name: Lithium iron disulfide
electrolyte: Lithium salt in organic solvent (ethers such as DME and 1,3-dioxolane)
self_discharge: About 95% of capacity retained after 20 or more years of storage (Energizer L91/L92)
summary: Lithium iron disulfide cells pair a lithium metal anode with an iron disulfide cathode to give a 1.5 V nominal, voltage-compatible replacement for alkaline AA and AAA cells. They hold a flat discharge, work from −40 to 60 °C, and weigh about a third less than alkaline.
body:
## How it works

The lithium iron disulfide cell is a primary lithium cell built to match the voltage of alkaline AA and AAA batteries. Energizer's L91/L92 handbook describes a spirally wound jellyroll of a lithium metal anode and an iron disulfide cathode coated on aluminum foil, separated by a microporous polyolefin film, with an electrolyte of a lithium salt in organic ethers including 1,2-dimethoxyethane (DME) and 1,3-dioxolane. The jellyroll gives almost 20 times the interfacial electrode area of an alkaline bobbin cell. Discharge proceeds in two steps: 2Li + FeS2 → Li2FeS2, then 2Li + Li2FeS2 → Fe + 2Li2S. Each cell also carries a vent and a PTC device that limits current when the cell heats above about 85 °C.

## Discharge behavior

A fresh cell reads 1.79 to 1.83 V open circuit; Energizer treats an open-circuit reading under 1.70 V as a sign of a discharged cell. Under load the curve is flat, close to 1.5 V for most of its life, and the cell's low effective internal resistance, about 100 mΩ, lets an AA deliver pulses of up to 3 A. Energizer recommends a 0.8 V cutoff and warns against discharging below 0.5 V. The advantage over alkaline grows with drain. At about 200 mA Energizer gives a specific energy of about 297 Wh/kg for its AA, against about 143 Wh/kg for a comparable alkaline. The cell is rated for operation and storage from −40 to 60 °C and keeps about 95% of its capacity after 20 or more years of storage.

## Uses

The chemistry is sold in AA (FR6) and AAA (FR03) sizes. Energizer positions it for high-drain and extreme-temperature applications, and as a lighter alternative where weight matters: its AA is 33% lighter than an alkaline AA.

## History

Energizer introduced the first 1.5 V AA lithium cell in 1989 and the AAA version in 2004. Wikipedia lists the system as lithium-iron, IEC code F, at 1.4 to 1.6 V nominal and 1.8 V open circuit, and notes that it replaced the earlier lithium copper oxide (IEC G) voltage-compatible cell by the mid-1990s.

## Status

Current. In edition 14 of IEC 60086-1 (2026), the maximum open-circuit voltage for letter F was raised from 1.83 to 1.90 V.
strengths: Much longer service than alkaline at high drain
About 95% capacity after 20+ years of storage
limitations: Fresh open-circuit voltage near 1.8 V can exceed some devices' tolerances
Only AA and AAA sizes are common
safety: Contains lithium metal; it ships under the lithium metal battery rules (IATA PI 968 to 970)
An internal PTC device limits current when the cell heats above about 85 °C
Not rechargeable; Energizer advises against discharge below 0.5 V
